newsitem.title: ALBANIA: European aid experts visit Albania.
newsitem.headline: European aid experts visit Albania.

text.p: European relief experts meet Albanian leaders on Thursday to debate a possible foreign force to protect humanitarian aid for the troubled nation where, in the latest spasm of violence, gunmen sprayed bullets at a bus near the capital.

A passenger was killed and seven were injured when unknown gunmen opened fire on the bus in central Albania shortly before the start of an evening curfew on Wednesday, an Interior Ministry source said.

The gunmen escaped. It was one of the most violent attacks around the capital since a wave of near-anarchy swept the former communist nation this month following protests at the collapse of popular savings schemes in January.
Further south, much of Europe's poorest nation remains in the hands of armed gangs, rebels without a cause except for their demand that right-wing President Sali Berisha resign.

Prime Minister Bashkim Fino and other ministers are to hold a meeting on Thursday morning with 15 European experts headed by Dutch diplomat Jan de Marchant et d'Ansembourg. They hope to work out ways to ensure that emergency relief gets through, including the use of foreign police.
D'Ansembourg's team, on a second visit in two weeks, will also debate Albania's plans for elections in June and ways of bolstering democracy for the country's 3.4 million people.

But six European Union nations, who have sent military experts to Albania to spearhead work for a possible security force to protect aid, suffered a setback after they failed to secure an international green light for their plan.

The 54-nation Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), the continent's top security body, failed to approve a mandate for a military mission at talks in Vienna on Wednesday. "The meeting ended in disarray," one diplomat said.

It was unclear when the OSCE would meet again and the six EU states -- France, Italy, Spain, Portugal, Austria and Greece -- may now get bogged down in seeking authority from the United Nations or could take the riskier step of going in alone.

Non-EU members Turkey and Romania have also expressed willingness to take part. But acting solely on Tirana's invitation could expose them to charges of propping up Berisha if they got drawn into any shooting.

Fino insisted that any foreign forces would be "a very small number" and would help keep open the ports of Vlore and Durres and protect Tirana's international airport, which reopened for normal business this week.

"We are not saying that they will come to restore order and deal with the people," he said in an interview with Radio Tirana on Wednesday. "Our government has asked that these forces cooperate with Albanian police."
D'Ansembourg, also said any relief mission would "not involve thousands of troops... It will depend on how many (personnel) the Albanians themselves can offer," he said.
D'Ansembourg's team includes experts from the OSCE, the 15-nation European Union and its Commission and the 40-nation Council of Europe.
D'Ansembourg said the group would stay several days and start with talks on Thursday with Fino on "how we can start right now with emergency aid."
In Brussels, the European Commission said on Wednesday it had agreed to send two million Ecus ($2.3 million) worth of humanitarian aid to help victims of the former communist state's crisis.
In Washington, the Defence Department said the United States had completed its evacuation of nearly 900 Americans and citizens of other countries from Albania.
